title: Modify Authentication Process
summary: Authentication on every platform is handled by dedicated components: the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service and the Security Accounts Manager on Windows, pluggable authentication modules on Unix-like systems, and authorization plug-ins on macOS. This technique covers any adversary change to those components with one of two goals, either harvesting credentials as they are validated or bypassing validation so that no valid password is needed. The change may be a binary patch in memory, an added or replaced dynamic library, an altered configuration file, or a new registration in the registry or file system. Because these components sit directly in the logon path, an implant there can survive password resets and continue to grant access through remote services such as virtual private network gateways, webmail and remote desktop. Artefacts vary by platform but tend to be unusual module loads inside authentication processes, edits to module directories or configuration files, and authentication successes that no real credential change explains. Legitimate administration also modifies these components during upgrades, single sign-on rollouts and vendor patching, so defenders need file hashes, signer information and change tickets rather than the mere presence of a change.

beginner.definition: Every computer has a part that checks usernames and passwords when somebody signs in. This technique means an attacker changes that part. They do it either to steal passwords or to let themselves in without knowing a real password.
beginner.whyItMatters: This part of the system decides who is allowed in, so changing it affects everything. An attacker who edits it can keep access even after you reset every password. The change often hides inside a normal-looking sign-in, so logs alone may not show it. If you never check these components, a backdoor can remain for months without being noticed.
howItWorks: Windows uses the Local Security Authority process and the Security Accounts Manager to check logons.
Unix systems use pluggable authentication modules, which are small libraries loaded during sign-in.
MacOS uses authorization plug-ins that decide whether a requested action is permitted.
An attacker patches one of these parts or adds a new module to the sign-in path.
The changed part either copies the password as it arrives or accepts a secret value.
Access then succeeds without a valid account password, and it may survive a reboot if stored.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where a receptionist checks badges at the main door. Every visitor shows a badge, and the receptionist decides who may enter. Now somebody pays the receptionist, or swaps the badge reader for a fake one. Visitors still look normal, and the corridor cameras still show people walking in calmly. The fake reader quietly copies every badge that it sees. Nobody notices anything unusual, because the routine at the door never visibly changed.
takeaways: Authentication components sit in the sign-in path, so tampering there affects every account.
Track changes to authentication modules, configuration files, and registration keys.
Correlate component changes with change tickets and with unusual sign-in successes.

objectives: Name the main authentication components on Windows, Unix, and MacOS.
Explain the two goals of modifying authentication: stealing credentials and bypassing checks.
Describe the file, registry, and memory artefacts that such tampering leaves behind.
Explain why these changes support persistence across password resets.
Plan monitoring that separates legitimate upgrades from malicious modification.
